newsitem.title: HONG KONG: HK says first row with Chinese troops just a mixup.
newsitem.headline: HK says first row with Chinese troops just a mixup.

text.p: The new Chinese military garrison's first conflict with Hong Kong authorities was just a mixup, the government told parliamentary deputies on Friday.
A political row built up after a Chinese general accused colonial authorities of an insult when they refused to allow his car into a closed border area.
The government told a legislative security panel that miscommunication lay behind the incident when a Chinese commander, Major-General Zhou Borong, quarreled with frontier officers.

"Partly, there is the language problem. Then, it was the first time the chauffeur had driven past the border, and he did not know the procedures," deputy security chief Carrie Yau told the Legislative Council group probing the affair.
"As for the accusation that Major-General Zhou went through the border without a permit it is not true," she said.
An advance party of 196 PLA soldiers is in Hong Kong to set up facilities for the future garrison upon China's takeover of the British colony at midnight on June 30.
Hong Kong media reported Zhou complained to the government that he had been mistreated when he tried to drive through the restricted border zone.
Chinese and British officials say language was the root of the problem. Cantonese is the Chinese dialect spoken in Hong Kong while Mandarin is mainland China's official language.
British Governor Chris Patten has denied Chinese troops in Hong Kong get special treatment putting them above the law by allowing their cars privileged passage without inspection.

The customs department told the legislature panel it was withdrawing a controversial list of 29 PLA vehicles it had given to frontier staff after the incident. The list was issued to customs officers in order to avoid further misunderstandings.
Lawmakers said the list would send a wrong signal to border guards that they should not check PLA vehicles.
Hong Kong is to become an autonomous part of China, but a border will still exist between the territory and the mainland.
After the handover, however, the PLA will not be required to show permits or undergo checks by Hong Kong customs, according to a garrison law taking effect on July 1.
Many of Hong Kong's 6.4 million people view the PLA with alarm because of its bloody crackdown of a student-led pro-democracy protest in Beijing eight years ago.
